# Volume 5 — CHAPTER XXXIII. RUPERT IS—NOT—WHIPPED

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

“I believe there is a matter I should disclose to you,” Mary Stubbs remarked with an air of mystery.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0000 }

She was strolling arm in arm with Grace and Ida through the village, after they had met up at Mr. Flagg’s store. Ida and Grace traded glances that communicated, “Now something disagreeable is coming.” Little joy was ever found in listening when Mary Stubbs felt she should share things with them. They frequently questioned why their fondness for Mary Stubbs persisted—because they truly did like her, regardless of all else. Certainly, she proved to be an invigorating and pleasant friend as a rule. If merely she did not harbor those beliefs regarding her obligation to share things with them!
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0001 }

“Are you aware Clementine Ainslie refuses to wed your father due to her belief that you are all so untamed? Fearing her own inability to raise you properly, she rejected his proposal.”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0002 }

A hidden feeling of triumph made Ida’s heart leap. Hearing that Miss Ainslie was not going to wed her father brought her great joy. Grace, on the other hand, felt a bit let down.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0003 }

“In what way are you aware of this?” she inquired.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0004 }

“Oh, it is being said by everyone. I overheard Mrs. Kerr discussing it with Mrs. Doctor. Although they believed I was beyond hearing distance, my ears are as sharp as a cat’s. Mrs. Kerr mentioned she felt certain Clementine feared attempting to be a stepmother to you on account of the reputation you have acquired. Your pa no longer walks up the hill. Lionel Fairlie does not either. People claim Harriet jilted him simply to even the score because he jilted her a long time back. Nevertheless, Lionel is walking around swearing he will win her in the end. Furthermore, I believe you should realize you ruined your pa’s romantic prospects and I consider it a shame, since he is certain to take a wife soon, and Clementine Ainslie is the finest wife for him I can think of.”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0005 }

“It was your claim that all stepmothers were evil and mean,” Ida remarked.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0006 }

“Oh—well,” Mary said, feeling somewhat flustered, “I am aware that the majority of them are terribly ill-tempered. However, Clementine Ainslie is incapable of being particularly unkind to anybody. Mark my words, should your pa change his mind and take Emmeline Drew as his wife, you will regret not having conducted yourselves properly instead of scaring Clementine away. It is terrible that your bad name prevents any respectable lady from wedding your pa because of you. Naturally, I realize that fifty percent of the stories circulating regarding you are false. Still, give a dog a bad name. Indeed, certain people claim that Tobias and Rupert were the ones who hurled stones through Mrs. Stimson’s window a few evenings ago, whereas those two Garrick boys were actually responsible. Nevertheless, I suspect Rupert was indeed the person who placed the eel inside old Mrs. Carr’s buggy, even if I initially stated that I refused to credit it without stronger evidence than old Kitty Hector’s statement. I stated as much to Mrs. Kerr directly to her face.”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0007 }

“Grace exclaimed, “What was it that Rupert did?”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0008 }

“Listen, they claim—remember, I’m merely repeating what others are saying—so you shouldn't get mad at me over it—that one night last week Rupert along with several other lads was catching eels off the bridge. Mrs. Carr went by in her rickety old buggy that has an open back. And Rupert simply went ahead and tossed a huge eel into that rear area. As the poor old lady Mrs. Carr was going up the hill near Hollowmere, that very eel crawled out right around her feet. Believing it to be a snake, she uttered a single terrible scream, stood right up, and leapt completely over the wheels. Though the horse ran off, it made its way home without any harm being done. However, Mrs. Carr hurt her legs awfully bad, and she has suffered nervous fits ever since each time she recalls the eel. Look, playing that lousy stunt on the poor old creature was terrible. She is a good person, even if she happens to be as odd as Rufus’s hat band.”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0009 }

An exchange of glances passed between Grace and Ida once more. The Good-Conduct Club was the appropriate entity to address this affair. A discussion regarding it would not be held with Mary.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0010 }

“There goes your pa,” Mary remarked when Mr. Ashdown went by them, “and he didn't notice us any more than if we were absent. Well, I'm reaching a point where it doesn't bother me. However, some people are affected by it.”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0011 }

Although Mr. Ashdown had failed to spot them, he was not strolling with his customary dreamy and preoccupied air. He marched up the hill, filled with turmoil and grief. The account of Rupert and the eel had just been imparted to him by Mrs. Hector Twiss. Her reaction to it had been one of great outrage. A third cousin of hers was old Mrs. Carr. Beyond being outraged, Mr. Ashdown felt wounded and appalled. That Rupert would act in such a manner had never crossed his mind. He was not disposed to judge strictly any mischievous acts born of carelessness or memory lapses, yet this proved otherwise. There was an unpleasant quality to this. Upon arriving home, he discovered Rupert on the lawn, quietly observing how a community of wasps lived and behaved. Summoning him inside the study, Mr. Ashdown stood before him, wearing a look more severe than any his offspring had previously witnessed, and inquired whether the report was accurate.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0012 }

“Indeed,” Rupert uttered, his face reddening, yet he boldly returned his father’s gaze.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0013 }

Mr. Ashdown uttered a groan, having wished that the situation had been, at the very least, magnified beyond the truth.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0014 }

“Relate the entire situation to me,” he requested.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0015 }

“Over the bridge, the boys were angling for eels,” Rupert remarked. “Link Drew had taken a giant—that is, an extremely large one—the largest eel that ever met my eyes. Having landed it right at the beginning, he had kept it in his basket for a lengthy duration, remaining utterly motionless. Honest I did, I believed it was dead. Old Mrs. Carr then crossed the bridge in her carriage, labeling all of us young varmints and instructing us to head home. Truly, father, we had not uttered a single word to her. Therefore, once she returned from her trip to the store and drove past again, I was dared by the boys to place Link’s eel inside her buggy. Believing it was far too dead to harm her, I cast it inside. On the hill, however, the eel revived, and after hearing her screech, we watched her leap out. I felt terrible about it. Father, that is everything.”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0016 }

Though the situation did not reach the full severity of Mr. Ashdown’s fears, its gravity remained undeniable. “I must punish you, Rupert,” he said sorrowfully.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0017 }

“Indeed, I am aware, father.”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0018 }

“I—I have to lash you.”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0019 }

Rupert flinched. Being beaten was something he had never experienced. Next, recognizing the extent of his father's distress, he remarked brightly,
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0020 }

“All right, father.”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0021 }

Mistaking his bright spirits for a lack of feeling, Mr. Ashdown instructed Rupert to join him in the study once supper was finished, and as soon as the youth had departed, he dropped into his seat with another groan. His dread of the upcoming night was seven times greater than Rupert's. The unfortunate clergyman lacked any idea of what instrument he ought to employ for the boy's whipping. Which items served to whip boys? Was it rods? Was it canes? No, such things would be overly cruel. Would a wooden switch do, then? Furthermore, he, John Ashdown, was obligated to hasten toward the forest to sever one from a tree. The notion was revolting. At that moment, an image forced its way into his thoughts without invitation. The shriveled, nut-cracker-like visage of Mrs. Carr upon the reanimation of that eel came into his view—he envisioned her flying like a witch over the wheels of the buggy. Prior to catching himself, the clergyman chuckled. Next, self-directed anger seized him, followed by an even deeper rage toward Rupert. He decided to procure that switch immediately—and it ought to possess a certain firmness, when all was said and done.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0022 }

In the graveyard, Rupert discussed the situation with Grace and Ida, who had returned home recently. The thought of him being beaten—and by father, who had never performed such an action—appalled them! Nevertheless, they concurred solemnly that the punishment was fair.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0023 }

“It was a terrible action, as you are aware,” Grace sighed. “Furthermore, you failed to confess while at the club.”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0024 }

“I forgot,” Rupert said. “Moreover, it did not seem to me that any damage resulted. That her legs were jarred was unknown to me. However, my upcoming whipping will settle the matter.”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0025 }

“Is it going to be very painful?” asked Ida, putting her hand in Rupert’s.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0026 }

“Oh, I suppose it isn’t that bad,” Rupert uttered courageously. “Regardless, I refuse to weep, regardless of the severity of the pain. Doing so would cause father immense distress. He is already deeply upset. I only desire that I could administer a severe enough beating to myself so he wouldn't have to do it.”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0027 }

Once supper concluded—a meal where Rupert consumed very little and Mr. Ashdown ate absolutely nothing—the two of them walked without a word into the study. Positioned on the table was the switch. Selecting an acceptable switch had proven difficult for Mr. Ashdown. Having severed a initial one, he deemed it excessively thin. What Rupert had committed was truly beyond justification. Subsequently, he severed a second one, which turned out much too stout. At any rate, Rupert believed the eel lacked life. A third attempt proved more satisfactory; yet, when he retrieved it from the tabletop, it felt exceedingly dense and weighty, resembling a club more than a switch.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0028 }

“Extend your palm,” he instructed Rupert.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0029 }

Rupert flung back his head and extended his hand without flinching. Nevertheless, because he was not particularly old, he was unable to fully hide a small amount of dread in his eyes. Mr. Ashdown gazed down into those eyes—indeed, they were Cecilia’s eyes—her exact eyes—and they held the identical look he had formerly observed in Cecilia’s eyes when she had approached him to disclose something she was somewhat fearful of disclosing to him. Her eyes were present here in Rupert’s small, pale face—and a month and a half earlier he had believed, during a single interminable, dreadful night, that his young boy was dying.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0030 }

The switch was thrown down by John Ashdown.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0031 }

“Depart,” he uttered, “I am unable to lash you.”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0032 }

Rupert escaped toward the cemetery, sensing that the expression his father wore was far more painful than a thrashing.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0033 }

“Is it ended already?” Grace inquired. She and Ida had stayed clasping hands and clenching their teeth upon the grave marker of Pollock.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0034 }

“He—he refrained from whipping me entirely,” Rupert uttered while sobbing, “and—I would rather he had—and he remains inside, experiencing pure misery.”
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0035 }

Ida slipped away, for her heart yearned to comfort her father. Opening the study door as noiselessly as a little gray mouse, she crept in. Twilight made the room dark. Sitting at his desk, her father had his back towards her and his head in his hands. Broken, anguished words were being spoken as he talked to himself; nevertheless, Ida heard—heard and understood through the sudden illumination that comes to sensitive, unmothered children. She slipped out and closed the door just as silently as she had come in. In what he deemed his undisturbed solitude, John Ashdown went on talking out his pain.
{: #nw-v05-c33-p0036 }
